source: AI Video Bootcamp's Camera Language lesson - the angle/shot-size vocabulary the transcript teaches as the first of its three foundational camera tools (angle, shot size, lens), independent of prompt_bank.json's own named shot_presets.
note: Three independent axes - vertical position, side/relationship to the subject, and shot size. Unlike lighting's quality x source there's no natural contradiction between them (low-angle + profile + close-up is a perfectly valid real combination), so there's no conflicts list, and no techniques dict either - the three axes fully describe camera position on their own. `custom` typed text always wins over any picked axis. The composed phrase is meant to be typed straight into Compose's own Shot field as custom text, replacing the camera slot - EXACTLY like typing any other custom shot today, which means it can legitimately score the camera realism layer at 0/8 if it names no capture device. That's the gate working, not a bug - see ui/spec_editor.py's own shot tooltip, which says the same thing.

eye-level.label: Eye level
eye-level.phrase: eye-level shot, the camera at the subject's eye height, looking straight across
eye-level.note: The honest baseline - can feel intimate or confrontational depending on the moment, never neutral by default.

low-angle.label: Low angle
low-angle.phrase: low-angle shot, the camera below the subject looking up
low-angle.note: The subject towers over the viewer - powerful, heroic, sometimes threatening. On a scared child looking up at an adult, the same angle reads as fear instead.

worms-eye.label: Worm's-eye
worms-eye.phrase: worm's-eye view, the camera at the floor aiming straight up
worms-eye.note: Pushed all the way down from low-angle - incredible on a person, a car, a bike, a building.

high-angle.label: High angle
high-angle.phrase: high-angle shot, the camera above the subject looking down
high-angle.note: The subject shrinks - vulnerable, exposed, cornered. Can also just show order and control rather than weakness, depending on the moment.

top-down.label: Top-down / overhead
top-down.phrase: top-down overhead shot, the camera directly above looking straight down
top-down.note: The scene turns into geometry - rooms become diagrams, people become pieces on a board.

dutch-angle.label: Dutch angle
dutch-angle.phrase: Dutch angle, the camera tilted so the horizon runs diagonal
dutch-angle.note: The one angle that breaks the horizon itself - instantly feels wrong, tense, unstable, like something's off.

frontal.label: Frontal
frontal.phrase: frontal shot, the subject straight on to camera
frontal.note: Direct, symmetrical, iconic - if they look into the lens, they're talking right to the viewer.

three-quarter.label: Three-quarter
three-quarter.phrase: three-quarter angle, the camera slightly to the side of the subject
three-quarter.note: The most natural cinematic look - shape and depth without the flatness of frontal or the closed-off feel of a full profile.

profile.label: Profile
profile.phrase: profile shot, the subject fully side-on to camera
profile.note: Distant, locked-in, closed off - the opposite instinct from a frontal shot.

back-shot.label: Back shot
back-shot.phrase: back shot, the camera behind the subject
back-shot.note: Mystery - the viewer follows them into the scene, seeing what they see but not their face.

over-the-shoulder.label: Over-the-shoulder
over-the-shoulder.phrase: over-the-shoulder shot, the camera behind one person looking at the other
over-the-shoulder.note: How you shoot a conversation or a confrontation - whoever's shoulder is bigger quietly holds the power.

pov.label: POV
pov.phrase: point-of-view shot, the camera as the subject's own eyes
pov.note: Sell it with what they'd see - their hands, a steering wheel, the frame of their glasses, a helmet visor, a scope, a keyhole.

extreme-wide.label: Extreme wide
extreme-wide.phrase: extreme wide shot, the subject a tiny part of a vast frame
extreme-wide.note: About the world, its scale, and how small the person is inside it - perfect for opening a scene, or crushing a character with scale.

wide.label: Wide
wide.phrase: wide shot, the subject head to toe with plenty of space around them
wide.note: Reads the person and the place at the same time - put a threat in the same wide frame and the viewer sees the danger before the character does.

full.label: Full
full.phrase: full shot, the subject filling the frame head to toe with less surrounding space
full.note: About the body - posture, silhouette, the outfit, the stance.

medium-wide.label: Medium-wide
medium-wide.phrase: medium-wide shot, framed around the knees
medium-wide.note: A balance of face, hands, body, and a bit of the surroundings - the action-and-movement shot.

medium.label: Medium
medium.phrase: medium shot, framed from the waist
medium.note: The most versatile size there is, the natural distance of a conversation - but a whole scene on medium alone gets monotonous.

medium-close-up.label: Medium close-up
medium-close-up.phrase: medium close-up, framed from the chest or shoulders
medium-close-up.note: The face takes over but a little body and context stays - the shift from behaviour to reaction, the shot of connection and trust.

close-up.label: Close-up
close-up.phrase: close-up shot, the face filling the frame
close-up.note: The world disappears and you read the eyes, the breath, the smallest change - doesn't automatically mean big emotion, the same close-up can be cold, threatening, beautiful, or empty.

extreme-close-up.label: Extreme close-up
extreme-close-up.phrase: extreme close-up, just one part of the face or one tiny detail filling the frame
extreme-close-up.note: Maximum emphasis on one critical thing - a single eye, a drop of sweat, a finger on a trigger.
